name: Macedonius the Consul
bio: Macedonius, called the Consul, was a Byzantine epigrammatist of the sixth century and a friend of Agathias and Paul the Silentiary; the title consul in his case was honorary.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him, chiefly in Book V.

poems.title: Book V, 223
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: O star of the morning, press not hard on Love, nor because thou movest near to Mars learn from him to be pitiless. But as once when thou sawest the Sun in Clymene’s chamber, thou wentest more slowly down to the west, so on this night that I longed for, scarce hoping, tarry in thy coming, as in the Cimmerian land.

poems.title: Book V, 224
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Cease Love to aim at my heart and liver, and if thou must shoot, let it be at some other part of me.

poems.title: Book V, 225
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: My love is a running sore that ever discharges tears for the wound stancheth not; I am in evil case and find no cure, nor have I any Machaon to apply the gentle salve that I need. JI am Telephus, my child; be thou faithful Achilles and staunch with thy beauty the desire wherewith thy beauty smote me

poems.title: Book V, 227
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Every year is the vintage, and none in gathering the grapes looks with reluctance on the curling tendrils. But thee, the rosy-armed, the crown of my devotion, I hold enchained in the gentle knot of my arms, and gather the vintage of love. No other summer, no spring do I hope to see, for thou art entirely full of delight. So may thy prime endure for ever, and if some crooked tendril of a wrinkle comes, I will suffer it, for that I love thee.

poems.title: Book V, 229
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: A herdsman, looking on Niobe weeping, wondered how a rock could shed tears. But Euippe’s heart, the living stone, takes no pity on me lamenting through the misty darkness of so long a night. In both cases the fault is Love’s, who brought pain to Niobe for her children and to me the pain of passion.

poems.title: Book V, 231
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Thy mouth blossoms with grace and thy cheeks bloom with flowers, thy eyes are bright with Love, and thy hands aglow with music. Thou takest captive eyes with eyes and ears with song ; with thy every part thou trappest unhappy young men.

poems.title: Book V, 233
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: “To-morrow I will see thee.’ Yet to-morrow never comes, but ever, as thy way is, deferment is heaped upon deferment. That is all thou grantest to me who love thee; for others thou hast many gifts, for me but perfidy. “I will see thee in the evening.” But what is the evening of women? Old age full of countless wrinkles.

poems.title: Book V, 235
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Against my hope thou art come to me, who longed for thee, and by the shock of wonder didst empty my soul of all its vain imagining. I tremble, and my heart in its depths quivers with passion; my soul is drowned by the wave of Love. But save me, the shipwrecked mariner, now near come to land, receiving me into thy harbour.

poems.title: Book V, 238
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Why do I draw my sword from the scabbard ? It is not, dear, I swear it by thyself, to do aught foreign to Love’s service, but to show thee that Ares ! though he be of stubborn steel yields to soft Cypris. This is the companion of my love, and I need no mirror, but look at myself in it, though, being in love, I am blind. But if thou forgettest me, the sword shall pierce my flank,

poems.title: Book V, 240
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: I pursue Love with gold; for bees do not work with spade or plough, but with the fresh flowers of spring. Gold, however, is the resourceful toiler that wins Aphrodite's honey.

poems.title: Book V, 243
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: I held the laughter-loving girl clasped in my arms in a dream. She yielded herself entirely to me and offered no protest to any of my caprices. But some jealous Love lay in ambush for me even at night, and frightening sleep away spilt my cup of bliss. So even in the dreams of my sleep Love envies me the sweet attainment of my desire.

poems.title: Book V, 245
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: You titter and neigh like a mare that courts the male; you make quiet signs to me; you do everything to excite me, but in vain. I swore, I swore with three stones in my hand! that I would never look with kindly eyes on the hard-hearted girl. Practise kissing by yourself and smack your lips, that pout in naked shamelessness, but are linked to no man’s. But I go another way, for there are other better partners in the sports of Cypris.

poems.title: Book V, 247
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Constance (Parmenis) in name but not in deed! When I heard your pretty name I thought you might be, but to me you are more cruel than death. You fly from him who loves you and you pursue him who loves you not, that when he loves you, you may fly from him too in turn. Your mouth is a hook with madness in its tip: I bit, and straight it holds me hanging from its rosy lips.

poems.title: Book V, 271
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: She who once frolicked among the fairest of her sex, dancing with her golden castanettes and displaying her finery, is now worn by old age and pitiless disease. Her lovers, who once ran to welcome her, the eagerly desired, now shudder at her, and that waxing moon has waned away, since it never comes into conjunction.

poems.title: Book VI, 30
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: O Amyntichus, his toil on the deep over, bound his lead-weighted net round his fishing spear, and to Poseidon and the salt sea wave said, shedding tears, “Thou knowest, Lord, that I am weary with toil, and now in my evil old age wasting Poverty, from whom there is no release, is in her youthful prime. Feed the old man while he yet breathes, but from the land as he wishes, thou who art Lord over both land and sea.”

poems.title: Book VI, 40
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: The two oxen are mine and they helped to grow the corn. Be kind, Demeter, and receive them, though they be of dough and not from the herd. Grant that my real oxen may live, and fill thou my fields with sheaves, returning me richest thanks. For the years of thy husbandman, who loves the truth, are already four-score and four. He never reaped rich Corinthian? harvests, but never tasted bitter poverty, stranger to corn.

poems.title: Book VI, 56
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Lenacoras, a vine-dresser, dedicated to Bacchus an ivy-crowned Satyr overloaded with wine. His head is nodding and you would say that everything in him is drunk, everything is unsteady, the fawnskin, his hair, the ivy, his eyes. Art with her mute moulding imitates even Nature, and Matter does not venture to oppose her.

poems.title: Book VI, 69
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Crantas, after his many voyages, dedicates his ship to Poseidon, fixing it firmly on the floor of the temple. It cares not for the winds now it is on the earth, the earth on which Crantas, stretching himself at his ease, sleeps a fearless sleep.

poems.title: Book VI, 70
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: O Kine of the sea and lord of the land, I, Crantas, dedicate to thee this my ship, no longer immerged in the sea—my ship, bird blown by the wandering winds, in which I, poor wretch, often thought I was being driven to Hades. Now, having renounced them all, fear, hope, sea, storms, I plant my steps confidently on dry land.

poems.title: Book VI, 73
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: I, Darunis the piper, in my shaky old age, my idle hand now heavy, dedicate, now I have ceased from the labours of the fold, my shepherd’s crook to rustic Pan. For still I play on the pipes, still in my trembling body my voice dwells unshaken. But let no goatherd tell the ravenous wolves in the mountains of the feebleness of my old years.

poems.title: Book VI, 83
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Eumorphus, finding fault with his aged hands, laid his lyre on the tripod as an offering to Phoebus. He said, ‘‘ May I never touch a lyre again or carry the instrument of the music I made of old. Let young men love the lyre-string, but I, instead of holding the plectrum, support my shaky hands on a staff.”

poems.title: Book VI, 175
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: This dog, trained in every kind of hunting, was carved by Leucon, and dedicated by Alcimenes. Alcimenes had no fault to find, but when he saw the statue resembling the dog in every feature he came up to it with a collar, bidding Leucon order the dog to walk, for as it looked to be barking, it persuaded him it could walk too.

poems.title: Book VI, 176
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: I dedicate to Pan and the Dryads this dog, this bag, and this barbed hunting-spear, but I will take the dog back alive to my stable to have a companion to share my dry crusts.

poems.title: Book VII, 566
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Earth and Ilithyia, one of you brought me to birth, the other covers me. Farewell! I have run the race of each. I depart, not knowing whither I go, for neither do I know who I was or whose or from whence when I came to you.

poems.title: Book IX, 275
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.note: Paton’s index says No. 275 cannot be by Macedonius and that the name is corrupt.
poems.text: Coprus killed the boar on land, and the swift deer he took in the blue waves of the sea. Were there beasts with wings too, Artemis would not have seen him empty-handed even in the air.

poems.title: Book IX, 625: On another Bath in the Lycian Quarter (?)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Let my doorkeeper be the most faithful of men, keeping careful note of the time at which bathers enter me, lest anyone against his will see one of the Naiads naked in my waters, or Cypris with the longhaired Graces: “For hard are the gods to him who sees them manifestly.” ! Who would dispute Homer’s dictum ?

poems.title: Book IX, 645
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: I am Sardis, the chief city of Lydia, who stand under flowery Tmolus, by the stream of Maeonian Hermes. I witnessed first the birth of Jove, for I refused to betray the secretly born son of my own Rhea. It was I, too, who nursed Bacchus, and I saw him shining with broader flame in the lightning-flash. First in my fields did Autumn, the giver of wine, milk from the udder of the grape-cluster the golden juice. Everything combined to adorn me, and old Time often saw me envied by the most flourishing cities. ;

poems.title: Book IX, 648: On an Inn in Cibyra
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Native alike and foreigner are ever dear to me, for it is not the business of hospitality to enquire who, whence, and whose son.

poems.title: Book IX, 649: On the Same
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Piety built up this house from its foundations to its lofty roof. For Macedonius did not build it out of wealth gained by despoiling with the sword the possessions of others, nor did he weep, a pauper, over an empty and profitless labour, deprived of the return justly due to his outlay. As rest from labour awaits the just, so may the works of pious men survive.

poems.title: Book X, 67
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Memory and Oblivion, all hail! Memory I say in the case of good things, and Oblivion in the case of evil.

poems.title: Book X, 70
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: If the Hopes, the companions of Fortune, make sport of human life, delaying to grant every favour, I am their plaything if I am human, and being mortal, I well know [am human. But being the sport of long-deferred hopes, I am willing and pleased to be deceived, and would not in judging myself be as severe as Aristotle, for I bear in mind Anacreon’s advice that we should not let care abide with us.

poems.title: Book X, 71
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: I smite when I look on the picture of Pandora’s jar, and do not find it was the woman’s fault, but is due to the Goods having wings. For as they flutter to Olympus after visiting every region of the world, they ought to fall on the earth too. The woman after taking off the lid grew pale-faced, and has lost the splendour of her former charm. Our present life has suffered two losses; woman is grown old and the jar has nothing in it.

poems.title: Book XI, 27
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Royal, sweet-scented dust of Sorrento, hail, and hail, thou earth of Pollenza most honied and Asta’s soil thrice desired from which the triple band of Graces knead for Bacchus the clay that is akin to wine! Hail, common possession of wealth and poverty, to the poor a necessary vessel, to the rich a more superfluous instrument of luxury!

poems.title: Book XI, 39
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.note: Headed “Macedonius of Thessalonica”; Paton’s Index of Authors lists it under Macedonius the Consul.
poems.text: Yesterday a woman was drinking with me about whom an unpleasant story is current. Break the cups, slaves.

poems.title: Book XI, 58
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: I wish not for gold, nor for the myriad cities of the world, nor for all that Homer said Thebes contained, but I would have the rounded bowl overflow with wine and my lips be bathed by a perpetual stream. I would have the gossiping company of those I revere drink with me while over-industrious folk labour at the vines. That for me is the great wealth ever dear to me, and when I hold the bowl I care naught for consuls resplendent with gold.

poems.title: Book XI, 59
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: We deep drinkers, champions of Bacchus the king, will initiate the exploits of our banquet, the war of cups, pouring out copiously the gift of the Icarian god. Let the rites of Triptolemus be the concern of others, there where the oxen are and the ploughs and the pole and the share and the corn-ears, relics of the rape of Persephone. But if we are ever forced to put any food in our mouths, the raisins of Bacchus suffice for wine-bibbers.

poems.title: Book XI, 61
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: A physician, a foeman, stood by me yesterday when I was ill, forbidding me the nectar of the cups, and told me to drink water, an empty-headed fellow who had never learnt that Homer calls wine the strength of men.

poems.title: Book XI, 63
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Yet men who care for the rites of harmless Bacchus, cast away poverty by the hope the vine inspires. Let me have a punch-bowl for a cup, and instead of a cask a wine-vat at hand, the home of bright jollity. Then straight when I have drunk a bowl of my wine I will fight with the giants, the sons of Canastra, if thou wilt. I dread not the ruthless sea nor the thunderbolt, having the sure courage of fearless Bacchus.

poems.title: Book XI, 366
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: A parsimonious man, laying hands on a treasure in a dream, wished to die enjoying a rich sleep. But when after the shadowy gain of the dream he awoke and saw his poverty as it was, he went to sleep again.

poems.title: Book XI, 370
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: The mirror does not speak, but I will expose you who daub your counterfeit beauty with rouge. Sweetly-red Pindar, too, once censuring this, said that “Water is best,’ water the greatest enemy of rouge.

poems.title: Book XI, 374
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: Make your fleshless cheeks always smooth with white lead, Laodice (just, indeed, is the penalty you pay the people), but never open your lips wide, for who by cosmetic fraud shall fix a row of teeth in it? You have shed all the beauty you had; loveliness of limb cannot be drawn from a perennial fountain. Like a rose you flourished in the spring ; now you are withered, dried by the parching summer of old age.

poems.title: Book XI, 375
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: I sneezed near a tomb and wished to hear of what I hoped, the death of my wife. I sneezed to the winds, but my wife meets with none of the misfortunes of mankind, neither illness nor death.

poems.title: Book XI, 380
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “(A Reply to App. Plan. No. 314, which should be read Jirst)”.
poems.text: The high-born virgin Justice, patroness of cities, ‘does not turn her face away from gold that is associated with piety, but the very scales of Zeus with which he weighs every law of life are of solid gold. “Then did the Father hold out the scales of gold,” if thou hast not forgotten the beauties of Homer.

poems.title: Book XVI, 51
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text: We honour the boy Thyonichus with this statue, not that thou mayst see by the beauty of this monument how comely he was, but, good Sir, that thou mayst learn his achievement, and be emulous of such enthusiasm. This is he whose legs never gave way owing to fatigue, and who vanquished every adversary, him of his own age, the younger one, and the elder one.

poems.title: The Morning Star (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Morning Star, do not Love violence, neither learn, neighbour as thou art to Mars, to have a heart that pities not; but as once before, seeing Phaethon in Clymene's chamber, thou heldest not on thy fleet-foot course from the east, even so on the skirts of night, the night that so hardly has lightened on my desire, come lingering as though among the Cimmerians.

poems.title: Inconstancy (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Constantia, nay verily! I heard the name and thought it beautiful, but thou art to me more bitter than death. And thou fliest him who loves thee, and him who loves thee not thou pursuest, that he may love thee and thou mayest fly him once again.

poems.title: Slayer and Healer (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I have a wound of love, and from my wound flows ichor of tears, and the gash is never staunched; for I am at my wits' end for misery, and no Machaon sprinkles soothing drugs on me in my need. I am Telephus, O maiden, but be thou my true Achilles; with thy beauty allay the longing as thou didst kindle it.

poems.title: To the Lord of Sea and Land (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: This ship to thee, O king of sea and sovereign of land, I Crantas dedicate, this ship wet no longer, a feather tossed by the wandering winds, whereon many a time I deemed in my terror that I drove to death; now renouncing all, fear and hope, sea and storms, I have planted my foot securely upon earth.

poems.title: To Poseidon, by a Fisherman (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Old Amyntichus tied his plummeted fishing-net round his fish-spear, ceasing from his sea-toil, and spake towards Poseidon and the salt surge of the sea, letting a tear fall from his eyelids; Thou knowest, blessed one, I am weary; and in an evil old age clinging Poverty keeps her youth and wastes my limbs: give sustenance to a poor old man while he yet draws breath, but from the land as he desires, O ruler of both earth and sea.

poems.title: The Sacred City (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Beneath flowering Tmolus, by the stream of Maeonian Hermus, am I, Sardis, capital city of the Lydians. I was the first who bore witness for Zeus; for I would not betray the hidden child of our Rhea. I too was nurse of Bromius, and saw him amid the thunder-flash shining with broader radiance; and first on our slopes the golden-haired god pressed the harvest of wine out of the breasts of the grape. All grace has been given me, and many a time has many an age found me envied by the happiest cities.

poems.title: The House of the Righteous (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Righteousness has raised this house from the first foundation even to the lofty roof; for Macedonius fashioned not his wealth by heaping up from the possessions of others with plundering sword, nor has any poor man here wept over his vain and profitless toil, being robbed of his most just hire; and as rest from labour is kept inviolate by the just man, so let the works of pious mortals endure.

poems.title: To-Morrow (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: "To-morrow I will look on thee"--but that never comes for us, while the accustomed putting-off ever grows and grows. This is all thy grace to my longing; and to others thou bearest other gifts, despising my faithful service. "I will see thee at evening." And what is the evening of a woman's life? old age, full of a million wrinkles.

poems.title: The Casket of Pandora (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: I laugh as I look on the jar of Pandora, nor do I blame the woman, but the wings of the Blessings themselves; for they flutter through the sky over the abodes of all the earth, while they ought to have descended on the ground. But the woman behind the lid, with cheeks grown pallid, has lost the splendour of the beauties that she had, and now our life has missed both ways, because she grows old in it, and the jar is empty.

poems.title: The Span of Life (Mackail)
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Earth and Birth-Goddess, thou who didst bear me and thou who coverest, farewell; I have accomplished the course between you, and I go, not discerning whither I shall travel; for I know not either whose or who I am, or whence I came to you.

poems.title: The Threshold
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Spirit of Birth, that gave me life,
  Earth, that receives my clay,
Farewell, for I have travelled
  The stage that twixt you lay.
I go, and have no knowledge
  From whence I came to you,
Nor whither I shall journey,
  Nor whose I am, nor who.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.223: Φωσφόρε, μὴ τὸν Ἔρωτα βιάζεο, μηδὲ διδάσκου,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Φωσφόρε, μὴ τὸν Ἔρωτα βιάζεο, μηδὲ διδάσκου,
Ἄρεϊ γειτονέων, νηλεὲς ἦτορ ἔχειν
ὡς δὲ πάρος, Κλυμένης ὁρόων Φαέθοντα μελάθρῳ,
οὐ δρόμον ὠκυπόδην εἶχες ἐπʼ ἀντολίης,
οὕτω μοι περὶ νύκτα, μόγις ποθέοντι φανεῖσαν,
ἔρχεο δηθύνων ὡς παρὰ Κιμμερίοις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.224: λῆξον, Ἔρως, κραδίης τε καὶ ἥπατος· εἰ δʼ ἐπιθυμεῖς
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
λῆξον, Ἔρως, κραδίης τε καὶ ἥπατος· εἰ δʼ ἐπιθυμεῖς
βάλλειν, ἄλλο τί μου τῶν μελέων μετάβα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.225: ἕλκος ἔχω τὸν ἔρωτα· ῥέει δέ μοι ἕλκεος ἰχώρ,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
ἕλκος ἔχω τὸν ἔρωτα· ῥέει δέ μοι ἕλκεος ἰχώρ,
δάκρυον, ὠτειλῆς οὔποτε τερσομένης.
εἰμὶ γὰρ ἐκ κακότητος ἀμήχανος, οὐδὲ Μαχάων
ἤπιά μοι πάσσει φάρμακα δευομένῳ.
Τήλεφός εἰμι, κόρη, σὺ δὲ γίνεο πιστὸς Ἀχιλλεύς
κάλλεϊ σῷ παῦσον τὸν πόθον, ὡς ἔβαλες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.227: Ἡμερίδας τρυγόωσιν ἐτήσιον, οὐδέ τις αὐτῶν
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Ἡμερίδας τρυγόωσιν ἐτήσιον, οὐδέ τις αὐτῶν
τοὺς ἕλικας, κόπτων βότρυν, ἀποστρέφεται.
ἀλλά σε τὴν ῥοδόπηχυν, ἐμῆς ἀνάθημα μερίμνης,
ὑγρὸν ἐνιπλέξας ἅμματι δεσμόν;, ἔχω,
καὶ τρυγόω τὸν ἔρωτα· καὶ οὐ θέρος, οὐκ ἔαρ ἄλλο
οἶδα μένειν, ὅτι μοι πᾶσα γέμεις χαρίτων.
ὧδε καὶ ἡβήσειας ὅλον χρόνον εἰ δέ τις ἔλθῃ
λοξὸς ἕλιξ ῥυτίδων, τλήσομαι ὡς φιλέων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.229: τὴν Νιόβην κλαίουσαν ἰδών ποτε βουκόλος ἀνὴρ
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τὴν Νιόβην κλαίουσαν ἰδών ποτε βουκόλος ἀνὴρ
θάμβεεν, εἰ λείβειν δάκρυον οἶδε λίθος·
αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ στενάχοντα τόσης κατὰ νυκτὸς ὁμίχλην
ἔμπνοος Εὐίππης οὐκ ἐλέαιρε λίθος.
αἴτιος ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔρως, ὀχετηγὸς ἀνίης
τῇ Νιόβῃ τεκέων, αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ παθέων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.231: τὸ στόμα ταῖς Χαρίτεσσι, προσώπατα δʼ ἄνθεσι θάλλει,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τὸ στόμα ταῖς Χαρίτεσσι, προσώπατα δʼ ἄνθεσι θάλλει,
ὄμματα τῇ παφίῃ, τὼ χέρε τῇ κιθάρῃ.
συλεύεις βλεφάρων φάος ὄμμασιν, οὖας ἀοιδῇ·
πάντοθεν ἀγρεύεις τλήμονας ἠιθέους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.233: αὔριον ἀθρήσω σε. τὸ δʼ οὔ ποτε γίνεται ἡμῖν,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
αὔριον ἀθρήσω σε. τὸ δʼ οὔ ποτε γίνεται ἡμῖν,
ἠθάδος ἀμβολίης αἰὲν ἀεξομένης.
ταῦτά μοι ἱμείροντι χαρίζεαι· ἄλλα δʼ ἐς ἄλλους
δῶρα φέρεις, ἐμέθεν πίστιν ἀπειπαμένη.
ὄψομαι ἑσπερίη σε. τί δʼ ἕσπερός ἐστι γυναικῶν;
γῆρας ἀμετρήτῳ πληθόμενον ῥυτίδι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.235: ἦλθες ἐμοὶ ποθέοντι παρʼ ἐλπίδα· τὴν δʼ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
ἦλθες ἐμοὶ ποθέοντι παρʼ ἐλπίδα· τὴν δʼ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
ἐξεσάλαξας ὅλην θάμβεϊ φαντασίην,
καὶ τρομέω, κραδίη τε βυθῷ πελεμίζεται οἴστρῳ,
ψυχῆς πνιγομένης κύματι Κυπριδίῳ.
ἀλλʼ ἐμὲ τὸν ναυηγὸν ἐπʼ ἠπείροιο φανέντα
σῶε, τεῶν λιμένων ἔνδοθι δεξαμένη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.238: τὸ ξίφος ἐκ κολεοῖο τί σύρεται; οὐ μὰ σέ, κούρη,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τὸ ξίφος ἐκ κολεοῖο τί σύρεται; οὐ μὰ σέ, κούρη,
οὐχ ἵνα τι πρήξω Κύπριδος ἀλλότριον,
ἀλλʼ ἵνα σοι τὸν Ἄρηα, καὶ ἀζαλέον περ ἐόντα,
δείξω τῇ μαλακῇ Κύπριδι πειθόμενον.
οὗτος ἐμοὶ πτοθέοντι συνέμπορος, οὐδὲ κατόπτρου
δεύομαι, ἐν δʼ αὐτῷ δέρκομαι αὑτὸν ἐγώ,
κἀλαὸς ὡς ἐν ἔρωτι. σὺ δʼ ἢν ἀπʼ ἐμεῖο λάθηαι,
τὸ ξίφος ἡμετέρην δύσεται ἐς λαγόνα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.240: τῷ χρυσῷ τὸν ἔρωτα μετέρχομαι· οὐ γὰρ ἀρότρῳ
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τῷ χρυσῷ τὸν ἔρωτα μετέρχομαι· οὐ γὰρ ἀρότρῳ
ἔργα μελισσάων γίνεται ἢ σκαπάνῃ,
ἀλλʼ ἔαρι δροσερῷ· μέλιτός γε μὲν Ἀφρογενείης
ὁ χρυσὸς τελέθει ποικίλος ἐργατίνης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.243: τὴν φιλοπουλυγέλωτα κόρην ἐπὶ νυκτὸς ὀνείρου
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τὴν φιλοπουλυγέλωτα κόρην ἐπὶ νυκτὸς ὀνείρου
εἶχον, ἐπισφίγξας πήχεσιν ἡμετέροις.
πείθετό μοι ξύμπαντα, καὶ οὐκ ἀλέγιζεν, ἐμεῖο
κύπριδι παντοίῃ σώματος ἁπτομένου·
ἀλλὰ βαρύζηλός τις Ἔρως καὶ νύκτα λοχήσας
ἐξέχεεν φιλίην, ὕπνον ἀποσκεδάσας.
ὧδέ μοι οὐδʼ αὐτοῖσιν ἐν ὑπναλέοισιν ὀνείροις
ἄφθονός ἐστιν Ἔρως κέρδεος ἡδυγάμου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.245: Κιχλίζεις, χρεμέτισμα γάμου προκέλευθον ἱεῖσα
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Κιχλίζεις, χρεμέτισμα γάμου προκέλευθον ἱεῖσα
ἥσυχά μοι νεύεις· πάντα μάτην ἐρέθεις.
ὤμοσα τὴν δυσέρωτα κόρην, τρισὶν ὤμοσα πέτραις,
μήποτε μειλιχίοις ὄμμασιν εἰσιδέειν.
παῖζε μόνη τὸ φίλημα. μάτην πόππυζε σεαυτῇ
χείλεσι γυμνοτάτοις, οὔ τινι μισγομένοις.
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἑτέρην ὁδὸν ἔρχομαι· εἰσὶ γὰρ ἄλλαι
κρέσσονες εὐλέκτρου Κύπριδος ἐργάτιδες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.247: Παρμενὶς οὐκ ἔργῳ· τὸ μὲν οὔνομα καλὸν ἀκούσας
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Παρμενὶς οὐκ ἔργῳ· τὸ μὲν οὔνομα καλὸν ἀκούσας
ὠισάμην σὺ δέ μοι πικροτέρη θανάτου·
καὶ φεύγεις φιλέοντα, καὶ οὐ φιλέοντα διώκεις,
ὄφρα πάλιν κεῖνον καὶ φιλέοντα φύγῃς.
κεντρομανὲς δʼ ἄγκιστρον ἔφυ στόμα, καί με δακόντα
εὐθὺς ἔχει ῥοδέου χείλεος ἐκκρεμέα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.271: τήν ποτε βακχεύουσαν ἐν εἴδεϊ θηλυτεράων,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τήν ποτε βακχεύουσαν ἐν εἴδεϊ θηλυτεράων,
τὴν χρυσέῳ κροτάλῳ σειομένην σπατάλην,
γῆρας ἔχει καὶ νοῦσος ἀμείλιχος· οἱ δὲ φιληταί,
οἵ ποτε τριλλίστως ἀντίον ἐρχόμενοι
νῦν μέγα πεφρίκασι· τὸ δʼ αὐξοσέληνον ἐκεῖνο
ἐξέλιπεν, συνόδου μηκέτι γινομένης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.30: δίκτυον ἀκρομόλιβδον Ἀμύντιχος ἀμφὶ τριαίνῃ
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
δίκτυον ἀκρομόλιβδον Ἀμύντιχος ἀμφὶ τριαίνῃ
δῆσε γέρων, ἁλίων παυσάμενος καμάτων,
ἐς δὲ Ποσειδάωνα καὶ ἁλμυρὸν οἶδμα θαλάσσης
εἶπεν, ἀποσπένδων δάκρυον ἐκ βλεφάρων
“ οἶσθα, μάκαρ· κέκμηκα· κακοῦ δʼ ἐπὶ γήραος ἡμῖν
ἄλλυτος ἡβάσκει γυιοτακὴς πενίη.
θρέψον ἔτι σπαῖρον τὸ γερόντιον, ἀλλʼ ἀπὸ γαίης,
ὡς ἐθέλει, μεδέων κἀν χθονὶ κἀν πελάγει. ”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.40: τὼ βόε μοι· σῖτον δὲ τετεύχατον ἵλαθι, Δηοῖ,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τὼ βόε μοι· σῖτον δὲ τετεύχατον ἵλαθι, Δηοῖ,
δέχνυσο δʼ ἐκ μάζης, οὐκ ἀπὸ βουκολίων
δὸς δὲ βόε ζώειν ἐτύμω, καὶ πλῆσον ἀρούρας
δράγματος, ὀλβίστην ἀντιδιδοῦσα χάριν.
σῷ γὰρ ἀρουροπόνῳ Φιλαλήθεϊ τέτρατος ἤδη
ὀκτάδος ἑνδεκάτης ἐστὶ φίλος λυκάβας,
οὐδέποτʼ ἀμήσαντι Κορινθικόν, οὔ ποτε πικρᾶς
τῆς ἀφιλοσταχύου γευσαμένῳ πενίης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.56: Κισσοκόμαν Βρομίῳ Σάτυρον σεσαλαγμένον οἴνῳ
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Κισσοκόμαν Βρομίῳ Σάτυρον σεσαλαγμένον οἴνῳ
ἀμπελοεργὸς ἀνὴρ ἄνθετο Ληναγόρας·
τῷ δὲ καρηβαρέοντι δορήν, τρίχα, κισσόν, ὀπώπην,
πάντα λέγοις μεθύειν, πάντα συνεκλέλυται·
καὶ φύσιν ἀφθόγγοισι τύποις μιμήσατο τέχνη,
ὕλης ἀντιλέγειν μηδὲν ἀνασχομένης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.69: νῆα Ποσειδάωνι πολύπλανος ἄνθετο Κράντας,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
νῆα Ποσειδάωνι πολύπλανος ἄνθετο Κράντας,
ἔμπεδον ἐς νηοῦ πέζαν ἐρεισάμενος,
αὔρης οὐκ ἀλέγουσαν ἐπὶ χθονός· ἧς ἔπι Κράντας
εὐρὺς ἀνακλινθεὶς ἄτρομον ὕπνον ἔχει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.70: νῆά σοι, ὦ πόντου βασιλεῦ καὶ κοίρανε γαίης,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
νῆά σοι, ὦ πόντου βασιλεῦ καὶ κοίρανε γαίης,
ἀντίθεμαι Κράντας, μηκέτι τεγγομένην,
νῆα, πολυπλανέων ἀνέμων πτερόν, ἧς ἔπι δειλὸς
πολλάκις ὠισάμην εἰσελάαν Ἀίδῃ·
πάντα δʼ ἀπειπάμενος, φόβον, ἐλπίδα, πόντον, ἀέλλας,
πιστὸν ὑπὲρ γαίης ἴχνιον ἡδρασάμην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.73: Δάφνις ὁ συρικτὰς τρομερῷ περὶ γήραϊ κάμνων,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Δάφνις ὁ συρικτὰς τρομερῷ περὶ γήραϊ κάμνων,
χειρὸς ἀεργηλᾶς τάνδε βαρυνομένας
Πανὶ φιλαγραύλῳ νομίαν ἀνέθηκε κορύναν,
γήραϊ ποιμενίων παυσάμενος καμάτων.
εἰσέτι γὰρ σύριγγι μελίσδομαι, εἰσέτι φωνὰ
ἄτρομος ἐν τρομερῷ σώματι ναιετάει.
ἀλλὰ λύκοις σίντῃσιν ἀνʼ οὔρεα μή τις ἐμεῖο
αἰπόλος ἀγγείλῃ γήραος ἀδρανίην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.83: τὴν κιθάρην Εὔμολπος ἐπὶ τριπόδων ποτὲ Φοίβῳ
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τὴν κιθάρην Εὔμολπος ἐπὶ τριπόδων ποτὲ Φοίβῳ
ἄνθετο, γηραλέην χεῖρʼ ἐπιμεμφόμενος,
εἶπε δέ· “μὴ ψαύσαιμι λύρης ἔτι, μηδʼ ἐθελήσω
τῆς πάρος ἁρμονίης ἐμμελέτημα φέρειν .
ἠϊθέοις μελέτω κιθάρης μίτος· ἀντὶ δὲ πλήκτρου
σκηπανίῳ τρομερὰς χεῖρας ἐρεισάμεθα. ”

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.175: τὸν κύνα, τὸν πάσης κρατερῆς ἐπιΐδμονα θήρης,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τὸν κύνα, τὸν πάσης κρατερῆς ἐπιΐδμονα θήρης,
ἔξεσε μὲν Λεύκων, ἄνθετο δʼ Ἀλκιμένης.
Ἀλκιμένης δʼ οὐχ εὗρε τί μέμψεται· ὡς δʼ ἴδʼ ὁμοίην
εἰκόνα παντοίῳ σχήματι φαινομένην,
κλοιὸν ἔχων πέλας ἦλθε, λέγων Λεύκωνι κελεύειν
τῷ κυνὶ καὶ βαίνειν πεῖθε γὰρ ὡς ὑλάων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.176: τὸν κύνα, τὰν πήραν τε καὶ ἀγκυλόδοντα σίγυνον,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τὸν κύνα, τὰν πήραν τε καὶ ἀγκυλόδοντα σίγυνον,
Πανί τε καὶ Νύμφαις ἀντίθεμαι Δρυάσιν·
τὸν κύνα δὲ ζώοντα πάλιν ποτὶ ταὔλιον ἄξω,
ξηρὰς εἰς ἀκόλους ξυνὸν ἔχειν ἕταρον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.566: γαῖα, καὶ Εἰλείθυια, σὺ μὲν τέκες, ἡ δὲ καλύπτεις·
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
γαῖα, καὶ Εἰλείθυια, σὺ μὲν τέκες, ἡ δὲ καλύπτεις·
χαίρετον ἀμφοτέρας ἤνυσα τὸ στάδιον.
εἶμι δέ, μὴ νοέων πόθι νίσομαι· οὐδὲ γὰρ ὑμέας
ἢ τίνος ἢ τίς ἐὼν οἶδα πόθεν μετέβην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.625: πιστότατος μερόπων τις ἔοι πυλαωρὸς ἐμεῖο,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
πιστότατος μερόπων τις ἔοι πυλαωρὸς ἐμεῖο,
κρίνων λουομένων καιρὸν ἐσηλυσίης,
μή τινα Νηιάδων τις ἐμοῖς ἐνὶ χεύμασι γυμνήν,
ἢ μετὰ καλλικόμων Κύπριν ἴδοι Χαρίτων
οὐκ ἐθέλων χαλεποὶ δὲ θεοὶ φαίνεσθαι ἐναργεῖς·
τίς γὰρ Ὁμηρείοις ἀντιφέροιτο λόγοις;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.645: Τμώλῳ ὑπʼ ἀνθεμόεντι, ῥοὴν πάρα Μαίονος Ἕρμου,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Τμώλῳ ὑπʼ ἀνθεμόεντι, ῥοὴν πάρα Μαίονος Ἕρμου,
Σάρδιες, ἡ Λυδῶν ἔξοχός εἰμι πόλις.
μάρτυς ἐγὼ πρώτη γενόμην Διός· οὐ γὰρ ἐλέγχειν
λάθριον υἷα Ῥέης ἤθελον ἡμετέρης.
αὐτὴ καὶ Βρομίῳ γενόμην τροφός· ἐν δὲ κεραυνῷ
ἔδρακον εὐρυτέρῳ φωτὶ φαεινόμενον·
πρώταις δʼ ἡμετέρῃσιν ἐν ὀργάσιν οἰνὰς ὀπώρη
οὔθατος ἐκ βοτρύων ξανθὸν ἄμελξε γάνος.
πάντα με κοσμήσαντο· πολὺς δέ με πολλάκις αἰὼν
ἄστεσιν ὀλβίστοις εὗρε μεγαιρομένην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.648: ἀστὸς ἐμοὶ καὶ ξεῖνος ἀεὶ φίλος· οὐ γὰρ ἐρευνᾷν
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
ἀστὸς ἐμοὶ καὶ ξεῖνος ἀεὶ φίλος· οὐ γὰρ ἐρευνᾷν
τίς, πόθεν, ἠὲ τίνων, ἐστὶ φιλοξενίης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.649: Εὐσεβίη τὸ μέλαθρον ἀπὸ πρώτοιο θεμείλου
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Εὐσεβίη τὸ μέλαθρον ἀπὸ πρώτοιο θεμείλου
ἄχρι καὶ ὑψηλοὺς ἤγαγεν εἰς ὀρόφους.
οὐ γὰρ ἀπʼ ἀλλοτρίων κτεάνων ληίστορι χαλκῷ
ὄλβον ἀολλίζων τεῦξε Μακηδόνιος·
οὐδὲ λιπερνήτης κενεῷ καὶ ἀκερδέι μόχθῳ
κλαῦσε, δικαιοτάτου μισθοῦ ἀτεμβόμενος.
ὡς δὲ πόνων ἄμπαυμα φυλάσσεται ἀνδρὶ δικαίῳ,
ὧδε καὶ εὐσεβέων ἔργα μένοι μερόπων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca X.67: μνήμη καὶ Λήθη, μέγα χαίρετον ἡ μὲν ἐπʼ ἔργοις
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
μνήμη καὶ Λήθη, μέγα χαίρετον ἡ μὲν ἐπʼ ἔργοις
μνήμη τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς, ἡ δʼ, ἐπὶ λευγαλέοις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca X.70: εἰ βίον ἐν μερόπεσσι Τύχης παίζουσιν ἑταῖραι
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
εἰ βίον ἐν μερόπεσσι Τύχης παίζουσιν ἑταῖραι
ἐλπίδες ἀμβολάδην πάντα χαριζόμεναι,
παίζομαι, εἰ βροτός εἰμι. βροτὸς δʼ εὖ οἶδα καὶ αὐτὸς
θνητὸς ἐών δολιχαῖς δʼ ἐλπίσι παιζόμενος,
αὐτὸς ἑκοντὶ γέγηθα πλανώμενος, οὐδὲ γενοίμην
ἐς κρίσιν ἡμετέρην πικρὸς Ἀριστοτέλης.
τὴν γὰρ Ἀνακρείοντος ἐνὶ πραπίδεσσι φυλάσσω
παρφασίην, ὅτι δεῖ φροντίδα μὴ κατέχειν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca X.71: Πανδώρης ὁρόων γελόω πίθον, οὐδὲ γυναῖκα
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Πανδώρης ὁρόων γελόω πίθον, οὐδὲ γυναῖκα
μέμφομαι, ἀλλʼ αὐτῶν τὰ πτερὰ τῶν Ἀγαθῶν.
ὡς γὰρ ἐπʼ Οὐλύμποιο μετὰ χθονὸς ἤθεα πάσης
πωτῶνται, πίπτειν καὶ κατὰ γῆν ὄφελον.
ἡ δὲ γυνὴ μετὰ πῶμα κατωχρήσασα παρειὰς
ὤλεσεν ἀγλαΐην ὧν ἔφερεν χαρίτων.
ἀμφοτέρων δʼ ἥμαρτεν ὁ νῦν βίος, ὅττι καὶ αὐτὴν
γηράσκουσαν ἔχει, καὶ πίθος οὐδὲν ἔχει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.58: ἤθελον οὐ χρυσόν τε καὶ ἄστεα μυρία γαίης,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
ἤθελον οὐ χρυσόν τε καὶ ἄστεα μυρία γαίης,
οὐδʼ ὅσα τὰς Θήβας εἶπεν Ὅμηρος ἔχειν
ἀλλʼ ἵνα μοι τροχόεσσα κύλιξ βλύσσειε Λυαίῳ,
χείλεος ἀενάῳ νάματι λουομένου,
καὶ γεραρῶν συνέπινε λάλος χορός, οἱ δὲ περισσοὶ
ἀνέρες ἐργατίναι κάμνον ἐφʼ ἡμερίσιν.
οὗτος ἐμοὶ πολὺς ὄλβος, ἀεὶ φίλος· οὐδʼ ἀλεγίζω
τῶν χρυσέων ὑπάτων, τὴν φιάλην κατέχων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.59: Χανδοπόται, βασιλῆος ἀεθλητῆρες Ἰάκχου,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
Χανδοπόται, βασιλῆος ἀεθλητῆρες Ἰάκχου,
ἔργα κυπελλομάχου στήσομεν εἰλαπίνης,
Ἰκαρίου σπένδοντες ἀφειδέα δῶρα Λυαίου·
ἄλλοισιν μελέτω Τριπτολέμοιο γέρα,
ᾗχι βόες, καὶ ἄροτρα, καὶ ἱστοβοεύς, καὶ ἐχέτλη,
καὶ στάχυς, ἁρπαμένης ἴχνια Φερσεφόνης.
εἴ ποτε δὲ στομάτεσσι βαλεῖν τινα βρῶσιν ἀνάγκη,
ἀσταφὶς οἰνοπόταις ἄρκιος ἡ Βρομίου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.61: χθιζὸν ἐμοὶ νοσέοντι παρίστατο δήιος ἀνὴρ
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
χθιζὸν ἐμοὶ νοσέοντι παρίστατο δήιος ἀνὴρ
ἰητρός, δεπάων νέκταρ ἀπειπάμενος·
εἶπε δʼ ὕδωρ πίνειν ἀνεμώλιος, οὐδʼ ἐδιδάχθη,
ὅττι μένος μερόπων οἶνον Ὅμηρος ἔφη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.63: ἀνέρες, οἷσι μέμηλεν ἀπήμονος ὄργια Βάκχου,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
ἀνέρες, οἷσι μέμηλεν ἀπήμονος ὄργια Βάκχου,
ἐλπίσιν ἡμερίδων ῥίψατε τὴν πενίην.
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ κρητὴρ μὲν ἔοι δέπας, ἄγχι δὲ ληνὸς
ἀντὶ πίθου, λιπαρῆς ἔνδιον εὐφροσύνης.
αὐτίκα δʼ ἡμετέροιο πιὼν κρητῆρα Λυαίου
παισὶ Καναστραίοις μάρναμαι, ἢν ἐθέλῃς.
οὐ τρομέω δὲ θάλασσαν ἀμείλιχον, οὐδὲ κεραυνούς,
πιστὸν ἀταρβήτου θάρσος ἔχων Βρομίου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.366: φειδωλός τις ἀνὴρ ἁφόων θησαυρὸν ὀνείρῳ,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
φειδωλός τις ἀνὴρ ἁφόων θησαυρὸν ὀνείρῳ,
ἤθελʼ ἀποθνῄσκειν, πλούσιον ὕπνον ἔχων·
ὡς δʼ ἴδε τὴν προτέρην, σκιόεν μετὰ κέρδος ὀνείρου,
ἐξ ὕπνου πενίην, ἀντικάθευδε πάλιν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.370: οὐ λαλέει τὸ κάτοπτρον· ἐγὼ δέ σε † πάλιν ἐλέγξω
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
οὐ λαλέει τὸ κάτοπτρον· ἐγὼ δέ σε † πάλιν ἐλέγξω
τὴν νοθοκαλλοσύνην φύκεϊ χριομένην.
τοῦτο καὶ ἡδυλύρης ποτὲ Πίνδαρος ἐλέγχων,
εἶπεν ἄριστον ὕδωρ, φύκεος ἐχθρότατον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.374: τῷ ψιμύθῳ μὲν ἀεὶ λιποσαρκέα τεῖνε παρειήν,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τῷ ψιμύθῳ μὲν ἀεὶ λιποσαρκέα τεῖνε παρειήν,
Λαοδίκη, λαοῖς ἔνδικα τινυμένη·
μή ποτε δʼ εὐρύνῃς σέο χείλεα· τίς γὰρ ὀδόντων
ὄρχατον ἐμπήξει φαρμακόεντι δόλῳ;
τὴν χάριν ἐξέρρευσας ὅσην ἔχες· οὐκ ἀπὸ πηγῆς ˘
ἀγλαΐη μελέων ἕλκεται ἀενάου.
ὡς δὲ ῥόδον θαλέθεσκες ἐν εἴαρι· νῦν δʼ ἐμαράνθης.
γήραος αὐχμηρῷ καρφομένη θέρεϊ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.375: ἔπταρον ἄγχι τάφοιο, καὶ, ἤθελον αὐτόθʼ ἀκοῦσαι
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
ἔπταρον ἄγχι τάφοιο, καὶ, ἤθελον αὐτόθʼ ἀκοῦσαι
οἷά περ ὠισάμην, μοῖραν ἐμῆς ἀλόχου.
ἔπταρον εἰς ἀνέμους· ἄλοχον δέ μοι οὔ τι κιχάνει
λυγρὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποις, οὐ νόσος, οὐ θάνατος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.380: παρθένος εὐπατέρεια Δίκη, πρέσβειρα πολήων,
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
παρθένος εὐπατέρεια Δίκη, πρέσβειρα πολήων,
οὐ τὸν ἐν εὐσεβίῃ χρυσὸν ἀποστρέφεται·
ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὰ τάλαντα Διὸς πάγχρυσα τελέσθη,
οἷσι ταλαντεύει πάντα νόμον βιότου·
καὶ τότε δὴ χρύσεια πατὴρ ἐτίταινε τάλαντα,
εἰ μὴ Ὁμηρείων ἐξελάθου χαρίτων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.51: τῷ ξοάνῳ τὸν παῖδα Θυώνιχον, οὐχ ἵνα λεύσσῃς
poems.author: Macedonius the Consul
poems.text:
τῷ ξοάνῳ τὸν παῖδα Θυώνιχον, οὐχ ἵνα λεύσσῃς
ὡς καλὸς ἐν τῇδε μνάματος ἀγλαΐᾳ,
ἀλλʼ ἵνα σοὶ τὸν ἄεθλον ὃν ἐξεπόνησε μαθόντι,
ὧ ʼγαθέ, τᾶς αὐτᾶς ζᾶλος ἔοι μανίας.
οὗτος ὁ μὴ κλίνας καμάτῳ πόδα, πάντα δʼ ἀγῶνι
ἅλικα νικήσας, ὁπλότερον, πρότερον.
